title: Ravana and Maricha's warning
hook: the king of Lanka hears the news, makes a plan, and is talked out of it on the first try
carry: pride stung in public is harder to talk down
tomorrow: Ravana and Maricha's warning, part two

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama alone defeated Khara's army and kept his promise to the sages, but Akampana escaped. One escapes to Lanka.

Until now, the Ramayana has spoken of Ravana without showing him. Now the story crosses the sea, into his city. Akampana arrives in Lanka shaking and tells the king of the rakshasas everything: Janasthana is empty, Khara and Dushana are dead, fourteen thousand lie on the field, and one man did it. Ravana's first response is rage. Who is this man? I'll burn him. And Akampana says: you can't beat him. But I know how you can hurt him.
screen: `ACROSS THE SEA, IN LANKA.` → `ONE MAN DID THIS.` → `I KNOW HOW TO HURT HIM.`

segments.voice: Akampana's idea is cold. Rama has a wife, Sita, and no woman in the world, he says, is her equal in beauty. Carry her off, and Rama will die of grief without a single arrow. Ravana likes it. He takes his chariot across the sea to an old acquaintance, Maricha, the rakshasa Rama spared years ago at Vishvamitra's sacrifice, hurling him out to sea alive. Maricha has lived as a kind of hermit since. Ravana asks for help, and Maricha says no. Whoever told you to do this, he says, is your enemy pretending to be your friend. Rama is a sleeping lion; don't go poke him. Go home, enjoy your wives, and let him live with his. And here's the surprise: Ravana listens, and goes home to Lanka. If the story stopped there, it would be about good advice taken. But Shurpanakha arrives at Ravana's court, mutilated, and she doesn't plead. She scolds. What kind of king are you, lost in pleasure while a man destroys your army and your frontier? You don't even know what's happening in your own lands. Then she describes Sita, at length. The warning that worked once is about to be overruled.
screen: `TAKE HIS WIFE, AKAMPANA SAYS.` · `MARICHA: DON'T POKE THE LION.` · `RAVANA GOES HOME.` · `SHURPANAKHA SHAMES THE KING.` · then, large: `PRIDE STUNG IN PUBLIC.`

segments.voice: Recall a time you took good advice, calmed down, and decided against something, and how it felt to let it go. Then recall a time your pride was stung in front of others and you wanted to prove something. Notice how different the two feel in the body, and let your breath slow and rest in the first.
Ravana, 'the one who makes others cry out': the rakshasa king who hears Akampana's plan, is turned back by Maricha, and then shamed into it by Shurpanakha.
Your line: pride stung in public is harder to talk down. Maricha's no held, until Shurpanakha spoke. That's day five hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Recitations of the Aranya Kanda that tell this part in full keep Maricha's first refusal, so listeners hear that Ravana was talked out of the plan once before Shurpanakha's scolding changed his mind.

original.note: Sanskrit rāvaṇa: traditionally explained as 'the one who makes others cry out,' the king of the rakshasas in Lanka.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ravana decides to steal Sita the moment he hears of her.
what it means: he's talked out of it once, and changes his mind only after public shame.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 31 gives Akampana's plan and Maricha's first refusal; Aranya 32–34 Shurpanakha's rebuke to Ravana as a negligent king.

chat.says: If Maricha talked Ravana out of it, why did Ravana go ahead anyway?
options: Shurpanakha shamed him in front of his court, and hurt pride is harder to calm down.
Maricha secretly changed his mind and urged Ravana to take Sita after all.
Akampana tricked Ravana into thinking Rama had already left the forest.
chat.meaning: Ravana listened to Maricha and went home. Then Shurpanakha scolded him in his own court, and stung pride overruled the warning.

notes: Maricha's 'sleeping lion' image and 'enemy in a friend's guise' paraphrased from Aranya 31; confirm.
The explanation of Rāvaṇa ('one who makes others cry out', from ru, to roar/cry) is traditional, given in Uttara Kanda; confirm wording.
The hook's 'first time we're in his city' is a narrative claim: Ravana is mentioned earlier (Bala Kanda) but this is his first scene in Lanka; confirm.
